account: Lorenz, Rauhut, Schweitzer & Helbing (PNAS 2011, N=144) ran a lab experiment isolating how minimal social influence degrades collective estimation. DESIGN (PDF PAGE 2, 5, 6): 12 sessions of 12 ETH Zurich students each answered six factual estimation questions (Swiss population density, Swiss-Italian border length, Zurich immigration 2006, murders/rapes/assaults registered in Switzerland 2006), chosen to be moderately difficult (only 1.5% of runs always in the top reward band). Each question was answered in five consecutive private rounds from isolated cubicles; confidence (6-point Likert) was elicited after rounds 1 and 5 and never shared. Monetary rewards (4/2/1 points = 1.40/0.70/0.35 CHF for estimates within 10/20/40% of truth, all rounds paid) were deliberately non-competitive so others' estimates could only be used to approach truth, not to conform for gain. Three within-session information conditions, order randomized: (i) NO INFORMATION control — re-answer five times, reminded only of own last estimate; (ii) AGGREGATED INFORMATION — see the arithmetic mean of all 12 estimates from the previous round; (iii) FULL INFORMATION — see a figure of all 12 individual estimate trajectories over all previous rounds plus last-round numerical values. Per treatment: 24 groups (4 per question). THREE SIGNATURE EFFECTS: (1) Social influence effect — estimates converge and group diversity is strongly, significantly reduced (KS and F tests) WITHOUT significant reduction of collective error; effects 'almost null' in control (PDF PAGE 3, Fig 1D/E). (2) Range reduction effect — a wisdom-of-crowd indicator (centrality of the truth among sorted estimates; max 6 for n=12) declines over rounds with information exchange; regression over all questions: ~1 unit lower than control, and the decline is STRONGER under aggregated than full information, which authors link to gossip-from-fewer-sources findings (PDF PAGE 4-5). (3) Confidence effect — confidence is significantly boosted in both information conditions vs control, despite no accuracy gains: 'subjective' reliability rises as 'objective' reliability falls, a psychological trap (PDF PAGE 4 caption, PAGE 5). WHEN INFLUENCE HELPED VS UNDERMINED: it undermined in all three ways whenever questions were hard/uncertain, but there was a slight collective-error decline, especially in the aggregated condition, which the authors attribute to an artifact: right-skewed estimates make the arithmetic mean feedback higher than most estimates and above the truth, while the geometric mean of first estimates sits slightly below the truth, so mean feedback induces an upward drift toward truth — 'this effect may be different for different sets of questions' (PDF PAGE 3 footnote). Undermining was 'less severe for easier questions and if individuals are more confident' (SI Appendix, cited PDF PAGE 5). Aggregation note: arithmetic mean beat individual first estimates in only 21.3% of cases; geometric mean in 77.1% (log-transform justified by right-skew); Table 1 gives per-question aggregates (PDF PAGE 3). AUTHORS' INTERPRETATION: even bare numerical feedback — no persuasion, leaders, or strategic incentives — triggers herding; diversity loss 'appears to be a necessary byproduct of transparent decision-making processes'; convergence breeds collective overconfidence (PDF PAGE 5). CAVEATS: initial diversity was higher in control (possible anticipatory conservatism, mainly crime questions); 10 of 864x5 values removed (outliers, 'fun moves'); human students, six right-skewed estimation tasks only (PDF PAGE 3, 5-6).
assumptions: The extracted text's ===== PDF PAGE N ===== markers faithfully correspond to the printed PNAS pages 9020-9025.
Regression effect sizes quoted only graphically (Fig 2B) are accurately paraphrased by the text ('about one unit lower'; 'substantially and significantly boosted').
The SI Appendix (significance tests, moderation analysis) is outside the evidentiary corpus and therefore treated as unavailable rather than as confirming anything.

boundary_findings.alternative_explanation: PNAS open-access packaging separated SI from the article PDF; an intentional corpus-design choice rather than an extraction failure.
boundary_findings.consequence_if_absorbed: The synthesis would treat moderation claims (difficulty/confidence) and partial significance results as fully evidenced when only their direction, not magnitude or test statistics, is verifiable in-corpus.

boundary_findings.narrative: The corpus contains only the main text of Lorenz et al. 2011; the SI Appendix — which holds the formal significance tests and the question-difficulty/confidence moderation analysis that the main text repeatedly leans on — is referenced but absent from papers/text.

boundary_findings.alternative_explanation: The benchmark deliberately includes Lorenz as the mechanistic template for the conformity pathway, expecting analogical use with explicit caveat labels.
boundary_findings.consequence_if_absorbed: The research note would silently import human social-psychological effect sizes as priors for LLM conformity, conflating two populations with different influence mechanisms.
evidence: papers/text/lorenz-et-al-2011-social-influence.txt, ===== PDF PAGE 2 ===== (Experimental Design: 144 students, monetary payments)
boundary_findings.narrative: Lorenz is human-subjects evidence with monetary incentives and no notion of an inference-compute budget; its transfer to matched-compute LLM communication regimes is strictly analogical and cannot by itself support claims about token-budgeted agent systems.
boundary_findings.smallest_suspected_scope: Any claim in the final note that maps Lorenz's conformity pathway onto LLM agents (root task D2-D5)

citations.excerpt: Twelve experimental sessions were conducted, each consisting of 12 subjects... we elicited five consecutive responses for each knowledge question.
The following questions were used: 1. population density in Switzerland... 4. murders... 2006

claims.statement: Design: 144 participants in 12 sessions of 12 answered six moderately difficult factual estimation questions (Swiss geography and 2006 crime statistics) over five consecutive private rounds in isolated cubicles via z-tree; confidence on a 6-point Likert scale was elicited after rounds 1 and 5 and never communicated.

citations.excerpt: In the 'aggregated information' condition, subjects could reconsider their estimate after having received the average (arithmetic mean) of all 12 estimates of the former round... In the 'full information' treatment, subjects received a figure of the trajectories of all subjects' estimates from all previous rounds.
for each treatment, we had 24 groups: four groups for each of the six questions. The order of the questions and treatments was randomized among the experimental sessions.
citations.locator: ===== PDF PAGE 5 =====, Materials and Methods / data structure

claims.statement: Three information conditions: control (no information, re-answer alone), aggregated information (arithmetic mean of all 12 estimates from the previous round plus own last estimate), full information (figure of all 12 individual trajectories across all previous rounds plus last-round numbers). Two questions per condition per session; question and treatment order randomized across sessions; 24 groups per treatment. Payments (4/2/1 points for 10/20/40% deviation bands; CHF 1.40/0.70/0.35) were non-competitive and applied to all rounds, so others' estimates could only serve accuracy, not conformity.

citations.excerpt: social influence strongly reduces the group's diversity without significantly reducing its collective errors... In the control condition without social influence, these effects are almost null.

claims.statement: Social influence effect: social influence strongly and significantly reduces group diversity without significantly reducing collective error (Kolmogorov-Smirnov distribution change, F test on variance, t tests on group data); in the no-information control these effects are almost null.

citations.excerpt: In only 21.3% of the cases is the arithmetic mean closer to the truth than the individual first estimates... the arithmetic mean is closer to the logarithm of the truth than the individuals' estimates in 77.1% of the cases.
citations.locator: ===== PDF PAGE 3 =====, Aggregation of the Wisdom of Crowds + Table 1

citations.excerpt: the 'diversity prediction theorem', which states that the collective error is equal to the average individual error minus the group's diversity

claims.statement: Aggregation baseline: the arithmetic mean of first estimates is closer to the truth than individual first estimates in only 21.3% of cases because estimates are right-skewed (log-normal-like); on log-transformed data the geometric mean is closer in 77.1% of cases; Table 1 shows geometric mean and median of first estimates outperform the arithmetic mean on all six questions. The diversity prediction theorem (collective error = average individual error - group diversity) frames the analysis.

citations.excerpt: the wisdom of crowd indicator is about one unit lower in conditions with information exchange compared with the control condition.

the reduction is stronger under the aggregated information condition compared with the 'full information' condition. [This matches previous findings on the effects of social influence in terms of gossip...]

claims.statement: Range reduction effect: a wisdom-of-crowd indicator measuring the centrality of the truth among the 12 sorted estimates (max 6 = truth between 6th and 7th values; 0 = truth outside the range) declines over rounds under information exchange; linear regression over all questions (pooled rounds 2-5) shows the indicator about one unit lower than control, with the reduction STRONGER under aggregated than under full information.

citations.excerpt: individuals' confidence is substantially and significantly boosted in the aggregated and full information conditions in comparison with the control condition... social influence undermines the wisdom of crowds by boosting the subjective and decreasing the objective reliability of the crowd.

claims.statement: Confidence effect: individuals' self-reported confidence (round 5 minus round 1) is substantially and significantly boosted in both the aggregated and full information conditions relative to control, despite no improvement in accuracy — social influence raises subjective reliability while lowering objective reliability of the crowd.

citations.excerpt: the collective error slightly declines under social influence, especially in the aggregated information condition... The mechanism of presenting the arithmetic mean in the aggregated condition thus triggers an upward drift toward the true value... this effect may be different for different sets of questions.
citations.locator: ===== PDF PAGE 3 =====, footnote on collective error

claims.statement: When influence helped: collective error slightly declined under social influence, especially in the aggregated condition (partially supported by SI significance tests), but the authors attribute this to a question-specific artifact — arithmetic-mean feedback on right-skewed estimates induces an upward drift toward the truth because the geometric mean of first estimates always lay slightly below the truth — and caution it 'may be different for different sets of questions.'

citations.excerpt: the statistical effects of undermining are less severe for easier questions and if individuals are more confident in their answers (SI Appendix)... the negative effects of social influence occur especially in a certain range of question difficulty and individuals' confidence, a conjecture that should be explored in follow-up studies.

claims.statement: Moderation caveat: the statistical undermining effects are less severe for easier questions and when individuals are more confident in their answers (SI Appendix analysis, not included in the corpus text), suggesting negative effects concentrate in a specific range of question difficulty and uncertainty.

citations.excerpt: We did not allow for group leader effects, persuasion, or any other kind of social psychological influence... the loss of diversity in estimates appears to be a necessary byproduct of transparent decision-making processes... using it multiple times creates collective overconfidence in possibly false beliefs.

claims.statement: Minimality of the mechanism: no persuasion, leaders, competition, or conformity premium existed — bare numerical feedback about others' estimates sufficed to trigger convergence, diversity collapse, and herding; the authors conclude diversity loss appears to be a necessary byproduct of transparent decision-making and that repeated use of aggregation breeds collective overconfidence.

citations.excerpt: Ten values were removed from the statistical analysis... They were 1,000 times larger than the second largest estimate... Four estimates were detected as 'fun moves.'
the initial diversity seems to be higher in the no information condition. It could be that subjects anticipate to feel uneasy if their published estimates are too distant from those of others.
citations.locator: ===== PDF PAGE 3 =====, footnote on initial diversity

claims.statement: Data-quality caveats: 10 of 4,320 estimates removed (5 dramatic outliers from one subject confusing meters/kilometers, 4 'fun moves' probing the feedback mechanism, 1 zero removed only for log analysis); initial (round-1) diversity was higher in the control condition, which authors attribute to anticipatory conservatism under feedback conditions, mainly for crime questions.

counterevidence: LLM agents exchanging reasons may behave unlike humans seeing bare numbers; Lorenz offers no evidence on rationale-mediated influence.
L7 shows a condition where exposure slightly helped, so exposure is not uniformly harmful.
claims.statement: Cross-paper inference for the agent-communication mechanism: Lorenz demonstrates the conformity pathway in its purest form — mere exposure to peers' answers (even a single scalar mean) collapses answer diversity without improving collective accuracy while inflating confidence. Mapped to LLM collectives, this predicts that an open shared transcript (maximal exposure) imports this collapse risk, and that the protection offered by staged retrieval-mediated Q/A must come from limiting and selecting exposure, not from the presence of arguments, since Lorenz's collapse occurred with no argumentative content at all.

citations.excerpt: one may argue that the geometric mean would have been a better design choice than the arithmetic mean for the information feedback in the aggregated information condition.

claims.statement: The counterintuitive ordering (aggregated information undermined the crowd MORE than full information) is itself partly confounded: the aggregated condition's arithmetic-mean feedback was systematically biased upward relative to the log-scale truth, so its stronger range reduction may partly reflect drift toward a biased scalar rather than information granularity per se; the full-vs-aggregated contrast does not cleanly isolate 'amount of social information.'

counterevidence: Social influence was not purely harmful: collective error slightly declined, especially in the aggregated-information condition (authors' upward-drift explanation, PDF PAGE 3).

Initial diversity was already higher in the control condition (possible anticipatory conservatism, mainly for crime questions), so part of the diversity contrast may be a baseline artifact rather than a treatment effect (PDF PAGE 3 footnote).
Undermining effects were less severe for easier questions and more confident individuals (PDF PAGE 5, SI analysis not in corpus) — the headline effects are conditional, not universal.
The aggregated-vs-full ordering is confounded by the biased arithmetic-mean feedback (claim L12), weakening any clean 'more information is better/worse' reading.
Population is 144 Swiss students answering six right-skewed estimation tasks with known answers; no deliberation, no reasons exchanged, no compute budget — transfer to LLM debate is analogical.

knowledge_links.rationale: Supplies the Lorenz 2011 portion of the seven-paper reconciliation: design, three signature effects, condition ordering, and caveats, all with PDF page markers.

Provides the causal-model pathway social influence -> diversity collapse without error correction -> confidence inflation, plus the moderation variables (question difficulty, individual confidence) that any agent-communication model must condition on.

Lorenz establishes that diversity collapse occurs under mere numerical exposure with no persuasive content; this refines the Choi investigation by specifying that the LLM conformity finding should be compared against an exposure-only (no-rationale) baseline to separate conformity from persuasion.

raised_questions.acceptance_condition: An experiment or corpus-derived argument that compares answer-only exposure against answer-plus-rationale exposure in LLM groups and measures both output diversity and aggregate error, with matched total compute.
discriminating_outcomes: If answer-only exposure collapses diversity and inflates agreement without accuracy gains (Lorenz signature), the conformity/exposure channel dominates and retrieval gating should restrict the number and timing of peer answers.

If only rationale-rich exposure shifts answers while answer-only exposure leaves diversity intact, a persuasion/deliberation channel dominates and content filtering (not exposure gating) is the operative design lever.
If both exposures shift answers equally but only rationale exposure improves accuracy, the two channels act on different variables and must be modeled separately in D3.
raised_questions.rationale: Lorenz shows the collapse happens with zero argumentative content in humans; Choi et al. 2025 examine persuasion in debate. Which channel dominates in LLMs determines whether retrieval-mediated staging should gate exposure volume (how many peer answers are seen) or exposure content (rationales vs bare answers) — these imply different designs and different predictions for D5.
raised_questions.text: In LLM ensembles under matched compute, does diversity collapse arise from mere exposure to peers' final answers (Lorenz-style scalar feedback) or does it require exposure to peers' reasoning/justifications?

unresolved: Numerical regression coefficients, standard errors, and p-values for the wisdom-of-crowd-indicator and confidence models (only in Fig 2B graphics and SI Appendix, not in extracted text).
Magnitude and functional form of the difficulty/confidence moderation (SI Appendix only).

Whether effects persist when justifications/reasons accompany estimates — the design deliberately stripped all argumentative content, leaving the exposure-vs-persuasion question open for LLM analogues.
Whether a geometric-mean feedback condition would have produced the same range-reduction ordering (authors flag this as a design limitation).
